title: PUT vs PATCH vs POST: REST API Methods Explained
description: The real difference between POST, PUT, and PATCH in REST APIs, including why idempotency is the key distinction that trips people up.
bodyHtml:
The three methods are often confused because they can all "change data," but REST defines them by a specific property: idempotency — whether making the same request multiple times produces the same end result as making it once.

MethodIdempotent?Typical use
POSTNoCreate a new resource; server assigns the ID
PUTYesReplace a resource entirely at a known URL
PATCHNot guaranteed, but usually treated as safe to retryApply a partial update to a resource

Why POST isn't idempotent

Calling POST /orders twice creates two orders. Each call is a new "create" instruction, so repeating it changes the outcome — that's the defining trait of a non-idempotent method.

Why PUT is idempotent

PUT /users/42 with a full user object replaces user 42's data with exactly that object, every time. Calling it once or five times in a row leaves the resource in the same final state — no duplication, no accumulation.

PUT vs PATCH, concretely

If you send PUT /users/42 with only { "email": "new@example.com" }, a strict implementation should treat that as the user's entire new representation — wiping out every other field not included. PATCH /users/42 with the same body means "update just the email, leave everything else alone." This is the single most common bug in APIs that misuse PUT for partial updates.

Quick decision guide

  • Creating something new, don't know the final URL yet → POST
  • Replacing a resource completely, know the exact URL → PUT
  • Updating a few fields, know the exact URL → PATCH
